title: Adverbs
intro: Adverbs add detail to verbs, adjectives and other adverbs. This guide shows how to form them and where to put them, then words that learners often confuse.

sources.label: British Council: Intensifiers so and such
British Council: Just, yet, still and already

sections.title: What adverbs are and how to form them
sections.summary: Adverbs say how, when, where or how often something happens. Many adverbs are an adjective with -ly.
uses: Adverbs of manner say how: She sings beautifully.
Adverbs of time and frequency: yesterday, soon, never, often.
Adverbs of place: here, there, upstairs, abroad.
Adverbs of degree: very, quite, too, almost.
Hard and late are also adverbs. Hardly and lately have different meanings.
Well is the adverb of good. Good is an adjective.

examples.text: He drove carefully through the fog.

mistakes.why: Use the adverb well after a verb.
Hard is also an adverb. Hardly means almost not.

checks.question: Complete: She plays the piano ___ (good).
checks.explanation: The adverb of good is well.

checks.question: Complete: He opened the box ___ (careful).
checks.explanation: Add -ly to make an adverb of manner.

sections.title: Where adverbs go in a sentence
sections.summary: The position of an adverb depends on its type.

tables.caption: Usual positions
head: type
position
example
rows: before the main verb, after be
She never eats meat. She is always late.
after the verb or the object
He drove slowly. He opened the door quietly.
after the verb or the object
at the end, or at the start for emphasis
I saw him yesterday. Yesterday I saw him.

uses: Frequency adverbs go between the auxiliary and the main verb: I have never been to Rome.
Do not put an adverb between a verb and its object: I like pizza very much, not I like very much pizza.
Place comes before time when you use both: We arrived at the station at six.
Adverbs such as already and still have special places. Read the next part.

examples.text: I usually get up at seven.

examples.note: Already goes between have and the participle.

mistakes.why: Do not separate the verb from its object.

mistakes.wrong: She goes always to bed early.
mistakes.right: She always goes to bed early.
mistakes.why: A frequency adverb goes before the main verb.

checks.question: Order: (the shop / yesterday / went to / I)
checks.answer: I went to the shop yesterday.

sections.title: Too and enough
sections.summary: Too means more than is good. Enough means as much as we need.

tables.caption: Position
head: word
pattern
example
rows: It is too hot to play.
too much + uncountable; too many + countable
too much noise; too many people
She is old enough to drive.

uses: Too is negative: it is a problem. Very is only a degree: The soup is very hot (maybe fine). The soup is too hot (we cannot eat it).
Enough goes after an adjective or adverb: fast enough, not tall enough.
Enough goes before a noun: enough time, enough money.
Use for + noun / pronoun and to + verb: It is too heavy for me to lift.

examples.text: The film was too long for the children.
Is the water warm enough to swim?
I haven't got enough money to buy it.

mistakes.wrong: He is enough old to vote.
mistakes.right: He is old enough to vote.

mistakes.wrong: There is too much people here.
mistakes.right: There are too many people here.

mistakes.wrong: I am too tired to not work.
mistakes.right: I am too tired to work.
mistakes.why: Too ... to already has a negative meaning.

checks.question: Complete: The bag is ___ (heavy) for me to carry.
checks.explanation: The result is a problem, so use too.

checks.question: Complete: We do not have ___ (time) to finish.

sections.title: Intensifiers: so and such
sections.summary: So and such make the meaning stronger. They are used with different words.

tables.caption: So and such
head: word
used with
example
rows: The film was so boring. He drives so fast.
It was such a boring film.
They are such nice people. It was such good weather.

uses: Do not use so before a noun. Use such.
Such a / an + singular noun: such a lovely day.
Result clause with that: It was so cold that we stayed in.
In speech that is often left out: It was so cold we stayed in.

examples.text: It was so hot that we went swimming.
She is such a good cook.
I have never seen such beautiful flowers.

mistakes.wrong: It was so a nice day.
mistakes.right: It was such a nice day.

checks.question: Choose: It was (so / such) a long film.
checks.explanation: A long film is adjective + noun.

checks.question: Choose: The music was (so / such) loud that I left.

sections.title: Just, yet, still and already
sections.summary: These adverbs often go with the present perfect and say something about time.

tables.caption: Meaning and position
head: word
meaning
position
example
rows: before the participle, or at the end
Have you finished yet? I haven't finished yet.
He is still working. I still haven't called her.

uses: Use just for very recent events.
Use already in positive sentences, and in questions to show surprise: Have you already finished?
Use yet at the end of negatives and questions.
Still shows that something goes on longer than you expect. With negative present perfect it goes before have: I still haven't found it.

mistakes.why: Yet goes with a negative or a question.
Use already in a positive sentence.

checks.question: Choose: He has (just / yet) left; you can still catch him.
